:::{#def-incidence-rate}
#### Incidence rate

Given a population of $N$ individuals indexed by $i$,
each with their own hazard rate $\haz_i(t)$,
the **incidence rate** for that population is the mean hazard rate:

$$\incidence(t) \eqdef \frac{1}{N}\sumiN \haz_i(t)$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-homogenous-incidence}

#### Incidence rate in a homogenous population

If a population of individuals indexed by $i$
all have identical hazard rates $\haz_i(t) = \haz(t)$,
then the **incidence rate** for that population
is equal to the hazard rate:

$$\incidence(t) = \haz(t)$$

:::

::: proof
By @def-incidence-rate,
the incidence rate is:

$$
\ba
\incidence(t)
&\eqdef \frac{1}{N}\sumiN \haz_i(t) && \text{(definition of incidence rate)} \\
&= \frac{1}{N}\sumiN \haz(t) && \text{(since } \haz_i(t) = \haz(t) \text{ for all } i \text{)} \\
&= \frac{1}{N} \cdot N \haz(t) && \text{(summing } N \text{ identical terms)} \\
&= \haz(t) && \text{(simplifying)}
\ea
$$ {#eq-homogenous-incidence-proof}
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-homogenous-incidence}
#### Incidence rate in a homogenous population

Suppose a population has $N = 3$ individuals,
each with hazard rate $\haz_i(t) = 0.02$ events per person-year.
By @def-incidence-rate:

$$
\ba
\incidence(t)
&= \frac{1}{3}\paren{0.02 + 0.02 + 0.02} && \text{(definition of incidence rate)} \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \cdot 0.06 && \text{(add)} \\
&= 0.02 && \text{(divide)}
\ea
$$ {#eq-homogenous-incidence-example}

which equals the common hazard rate, as @thm-homogenous-incidence says.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-heterogeneous-incidence}
#### Incidence rate in a heterogeneous population

If instead the three individuals have hazard rates
$0.01$, $0.02$, and $0.06$ events per person-year,
then:

$$
\ba
\incidence(t)
&= \frac{1}{3}\paren{0.01 + 0.02 + 0.06} && \text{(definition of incidence rate)} \\
&= \frac{1}{3} \cdot 0.09 && \text{(add)} \\
&= 0.03 && \text{(divide)}
\ea
$$ {#eq-heterogeneous-incidence-example}

which differs from every individual's hazard rate,
so the conclusion of @thm-homogenous-incidence
needs its assumption of identical hazards.
:::
